[Project overview]{.eyebrow}

::: {.lead}
The overall goal of this research is to understand plant-soil-microbe
interactions in response to a changing environment.
:::

This Alaska-based project initially focused on a permafrost thaw gradient at the
Fairbanks Permafrost Experiment Station. We set up controlled experiments to
test the effects of soil microbes on the growth of Alaskan berries. Plant growth
slowed with microbes from thawed regions relative to controls. These plant-soil
feedbacks may influence how the plant community responds to changing climatic
conditions.

We then dug deeper into the microbial community, profiling its functional
potential alongside an in-depth study of community structure across the thaw
disturbance gradient.

The lab has applied this work to understanding antibiotic resistance in the
environment. Identifying specific antibiotic resistant microbes is essential for
quick and appropriate treatment of Alaskans. Using culture-based methods, we
found widespread antibiotic resistance in local boreal forest soils affected by
thawing permafrost.

We have also worked with members of the US Fish and Wildlife Service and Los
Alamos National Laboratory to develop a collaboration for monitoring Alaska's
National Wildlife Refuges for microbial indicators and pathogenic vectors with
implications for human and wildlife health.
